LADE consists of three components: (1) Extracting Latent Safety Signals from Dark Knowledge, which selects top-k safety-discriminative tokens from the first-token probability distribution; (2) Tokenizer Mapping, which maps these tokens across different tokenizers to enable model-agnostic application; and (3) kNN-based Discrimination, which classifies queries via a k-Nearest Neighbors search over the mapped tokens. Across diverse LLMs and benchmarks, LADE is robust against a wide range of jailbreak attacks and lowers attack success rates while maintaining a competitive safety-utility trade-off.

items.title: REACT: Representational Early Analysis and Control of Chain-of-Thought Trajectories
items.description: arXiv:2610.32113v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) generation offers an opportunity to intervene before a reasoning model completes its answer. How does the safety effect of a single activation edit vary across early reasoning states, and what factors govern that variation? We study this question with REACT, a conditional activation intervention that learns a safety direction from paired safe and unsafe trajectories and applies it once to an early CoT hidden state. The model weights remain frozen, and all subsequent tokens are generated without further edits. To study timing, we train directions separately at each of the first five CoT positions and evaluate ungated edits with full post-edit regeneration. Across three DeepSeek-R1 distilled models, site-specific edits concentrate safety gains in the opening CoT tokens. Norm-matched controls on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B (8B) disentangle two factors behind this curve: holding an effective direction and edit budget fixed still yields much larger early ($t_1$-$t_5$) than later ($t_6$-$t_8$) gains, whereas the near-zero site-specific $t_3$ gain reflects higher optimisation variance despite rising risk-probe AUROC. Forced prefixes shift the high-gain region with the opening context, and a four-arm intervention shows that ~98% of the net gain at $t_2$ propagates through the changed next token. On the same 8B model, REACT raises the rate of fully safe CoT-answer outputs on StrongREJECT-273 from 29.06% to 82.05%, while keeping benign refusal and usefulness near baseline. An anonymized implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/REACT_official2-333B.

items.title: SynthDCB: World Distillation for Scalable Device Control Benchmarking
items.description: arXiv:2611.18639v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Scaling device-control evaluation requires scaling both interactive worlds and the tasks agents must solve. We introduce SynthDCB, a benchmark for environment awareness and device control built through world distillation (WD). World distillation transforms knowledge of device behaviors, constraints, and environmental effects into modular executable components. A unified capability representation connects tool discovery, world execution, and task synthesis. SynthDCB instantiates Home, Car, and Phone with 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events, supporting five task families with 32 subtypes. Explicit states and tool-call traces support task validation and agent evaluation. We evaluate 22 models on 2,560 test tasks; the best achieves 88.8% mean Pass@1. Construction experiments demonstrate token efficiency and expansion of task coverage. At the richest knowledge level, WD fully covers 22/23 properties, 19/29 functionalities, and 30/39 event requirements specified in a real RobotVacuum protocol. Furthermore, the 1,000 sampled tasks semantically cover 81.6% of the 854 reference instructions in the real-world corpus. SynthDCB connects an expanding space of real-to-sim executable capabilities to verifiable agent evaluation.

items.title: How to make a moral agent: sentimentalism and rationalism as lenses on AI
items.description: arXiv:2611.18714v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Can AI systems be moral agents? That is, can they undertake actions that can be correctly assessed as morally right or wrong? There is no settled normative criterion of moral agency that applies neatly outside paradigm human cases. Because of the difficulties with a normative account, we instead propose a research program to explore descriptive moral agency. Most basically, we ask, what are the capabilities we humans possess that underlie our moral agency? To do so, we draw on historical scholarship in philosophy and moral psychology to isolate candidate capabilities. Then we suggest refining candidate capabilities so that they are testable in the context of AI systems. Finally, we offer specific empirical recommendations to test AI systems, especially large language models (LLMs), for those refined capabilities. Our approach offers several benefits. Firstly, it may demonstrate whether the behaviors of AI systems are aligned, or in a broad sense desirable. Secondly, the debate may inform policy questions (e.g., what models should be deployed in which contexts?). Thirdly, our approach may complement engineering and design efforts: when capabilities can be precisely characterized, they can inform the development of models. Fourthly, applying our moral reasoning concepts in the new context of AI systems should improve our understanding of those concepts.

items.title: Geometry-bridge flow matching for blind rigid-motion correction in head cone-beam CT
items.description: arXiv:2611.23788v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Rigid motion of a patient head during head cone-beam CT (CBCT) scan can degrade image quality and complicate recovery of accurate anatomical structures from the measured projections. We present a 3D flow-matching prior approach that learns the image changes induced by motion. Its geometry-bridge connects motion-corrupted and motion-free Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) reconstructed images of the same source volume through progressively reduced simulated motion. The forward projector's geometry derivative supplies analytic velocity targets along this path. A plug-and-play loop encompasses the learned image updates together with spline-based pose estimation, conjugate-gradient data consistency, and image total-variation regularization. Both the refined image volume and the FDK reconstructed image volume at the estimated poses are evaluated. On simulated 360-view scans from 30 held-out CQ500 patients with nominal per-component motion amplitudes within 10 mm / 10 degrees, the framework achieved state-of-the-art image reconstruction quality and motion accuracy in comparison with other methos such as learned autofocus and diffusion-based joint reconstruction. Mean peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) reached 37.1 dB and mean detector-plane reprojection error (RPE) was 0.27 mm. With matched endpoints at the inference settings, the geometry bridge improved PSNR by 1.6 dB and reduced RPE by 33% relative to image-linear training. With 50 prior updates and coarse-to-fine motion estimation, total processing time averaged 9.1 minutes per patient on an RTX A6000.

items.title: PsyWorld: Profile-Conditioned World Modeling for Human Behavior Prediction
items.description: arXiv:2611.24999v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding how stable psychometric traits and time-varying states jointly inform behavior is an important problem in computational behavioral science. Existing personalized agents commonly condition actions directly on a static profile, leaving realized state transitions unused as an explicit source of supervision. We introduce a profile-conditioned state world model that uses observed environment--behavior state transitions to learn transition-informed representations for behavioral prediction. During training, a posterior encoder quantizes realized transitions, while a prior predicts the resulting codes from the psychometric profile and pre-transition context. The prior code and predicted next state then condition macro-level behavior and simulator-grounded execution. Thus, the world model provides structured transition supervision instead of treating personality as a direct action descriptor. We evaluate the framework in VEET, a controlled behavioral simulator with human trajectories, and in AgentSociety as a structurally different synthetic environment. A participant-disjoint split of 240 training, 25 validation, and 48 test participants evaluates generalization to unseen people. On VEET, the model reaches 0.904 Top-1 accuracy (95\% CI: [0.895, 0.913]) and 0.0033 Macro KL. Ablations associate continuous next-state modeling with most of the Top-1 gain, while discrete codes and prior alignment mainly improve Top-3 and distributional alignment. These results establish transition-informed world-model supervision as useful for subject-generalized behavior prediction, without implying causal psychological mechanisms or calibrated long-horizon state dynamics.

items.title: Watch Where You Linearize: Predicting and Correcting Model-Merging Interference
items.description: arXiv:2611.25000v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model merging combines separately fine-tuned models by adding their task vectors to a shared backbone. Interference is typically assessed only after constructing and evaluating a candidate merge, making coefficient search expensive. We show that a first-order directional derivative of task A's outputs along task B's vector can predict interference, but only when evaluated at the appropriate model. At the receiver model, this derivative forecasts nearby merges per task and per example, halves the accuracy error of a no-change baseline, and identifies most examples whose predictions flip. For full multi-task merges, a single evaluation is insufficient; two evaluations along the merge path are needed. At the shared pretrained backbone, however, the derivative is nearly orthogonal to realized changes in our vision experiments and only partly predictive in LoRA language-model pilots. Controls link this failure to displacement along the receiver's own task vector, not simply parameter distance; the mismatch appears within the first few dozen fine-tuning steps. Freezing receiver-local responses produces a surrogate affine in the merge coefficients. We use it to construct LR-Merge, a label-free correction that optimizes coefficients through convex teacher matching on unlabeled probes, without backpropagation through merged networks. LR-Merge improves all tested closed-form, isotropic, and sparsified base mergers, with gains generally increasing as more tasks are merged. Using pretrained rather than receiver-local responses instead degrades the base merge. LR-Merge matches exact teacher matching through a merged network, which takes roughly three times longer to converge and performs similarly at an equal compute budget. Once built, the surrogate answers new coefficient and task-subset queries in seconds.

items.title: Density Feedback Control for Transferability of Generative Sparse Adversarial Attacks
items.description: arXiv:2611.25001v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generator-based sparse adversarial attacks train encoder--decoder networks to produce transferable sparse perturbations for black-box robustness evaluation. Their perturbation density, however, is set only indirectly by a fixed sparsity coefficient whose mapping to density is unknown and shifts during training, so reaching a target density requires re-tuning; this fixed pressure also yields little transferability gain once density reduction begins. We propose Density Feedback Control (DFC), which tightens or relaxes this coefficient at the end of each epoch according to the gap between the observed hard-mask density and the target, without changing the generator architecture or loss. At a 10\% target density, DFC brings the mean density of three base attacks within one percentage point of the target in a single run and improves the transfer attack success rate (ASR) of two of them on CNN and Transformer targets, including under per-image $\ell_0$ budgets, while perturbing fewer pixels. Tracing GPG's training, we observe that as DFC relaxes the coefficient, the transfer ASR recovers with the density and overtakes the fixed-coefficient baseline with fewer pixels. For EGS-TSSA, which restricts perturbations to source-model feature-importance regions, DFC yields no consistent gain; we analyze how this restriction interacts with density feedback.

items.title: On the Impact of Feature Reduction Techniques on Adversarial Attacks
items.description: arXiv:2611.25004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adversarial attacks have posed significant threats to machine learning models by exploiting their inherent vulnerabilities. Researchers have established an interdisciplinary field called adversarial machine learning to explore these vulnerabilities and develop corresponding defense strategies. Feature reduction strategies are used to decrease the dimensionality of the data in order to reduce training time, avoid the curse of dimensionality, prevent overfitting, and mitigate redundant features. However, their effect on adversarial robustness across different classifiers and attack scenarios remains insufficiently explored. This study aims to analyze the effect of feature reduction techniques on the adversarial robustness of a diverse set of machine learning models under poisoning, backdoor, and universal adversarial perturbation attacks on the APT dataset. These models include support vector machine, decision tree, random forest, multi-layer perceptron, and k-nearest neighbors. The attained results are compared with scenarios where different feature reduction techniques are applied, including principal component analysis, permutation importance ranking, recursive feature elimination, and univariate mutual information. Metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, and mitigation score are employed to evaluate the effect of these techniques on adversarial robustness. The results demonstrate that permutation importance ranking and univariate mutual information generally provide the most consistent robustness improvements, while other methods exhibit more variable effects depending on the classifier and attack scenario.

items.title: Near-Quadratic Sample Compression for All VC Classes
items.description: arXiv:2611.25011v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The sample compression conjecture is a longstanding open problem in learning theory, originating in the work of Littlestone and Warmuth in the 1980s. At its heart is a connection between simplification and generalization: if a predictor consistent with a training sample is defined using only a small part of that sample, then it is likely to generalize. Sample compression schemes formalize this idea, and many natural learning algorithms can be analyzed this way. The sample compression conjecture of Floyd and Warmuth (1995) asserts that every binary concept class of VC dimension $d$ admits a sample compression scheme of size $O(d)$; a weaker conjecture asks only for size polynomial in $d$. Both have remained open: the first bound depending only on $d$, due to Moran and Yehudayoff (2016), is exponential in $d$. We prove the weaker conjecture by constructing a sample compression scheme of size $O(d^2 \log^2 d)$.

items.title: HapBO: Harnessed $\alpha$-$\pi$ Bayesian Optimization via Expert Natural Language Priors
items.description: arXiv:2611.25100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bayesian Optimization (BO) can be substantially more sample-efficient when informed by prior knowledge about the problem. In practice, however, such knowledge is often available only in natural language, e.g., expert intuitions or documentation, rather than as the explicit probability distribution landscape that prior-guided BO methods may require. Leveraging it effectively demands both an expressive mapping from language to priors and robustness to information that may be misleading. We propose HapBO (Harnessed $\alpha$-$\pi$ Bayesian Optimization), which elicits beliefs once from a human expert, a large language model (LLM), or both, and deterministically compiles a structured specification into a reusable belief function ($\pi: \mathcal{X} \to[0,1]$), with a rich representation not restricted to a Gaussian family. Building on $\alpha$-$\pi$BO, HapBO applies this belief function through a bounded positive multiplier on any nonnegative acquisition, preserving positive acquisition support and requiring no LLM calls during optimization. We prove that, for the Expected Improvement acquisition function (EI), HapBO preserves the standard simple-regret rate up to a bounded factor, even under adversarial beliefs. We evaluate HapBO on 40 HPOBench tasks, a synthetic suite in 6-15 dimensions and two real-world applications: cortical neurostimulation and constrained solar design. HapBO achieves the lowest aggregate HPOBench regret and strong real-world task performance, with zero in-loop token cost. In real-world applications it improves the optimization outcome even at budgets of 12-20 queries, and at a small fraction of the wall-clock and token costs of other LLM-based methods.

items.title: Long-Range Video Presentation Attack Detection: A Three-Class Benchmark Across 1-100 m and Two Sensor Types
items.description: arXiv:2611.25108v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Face presentation attack detection (PAD) systems deployed in border control and airport surveillance are constrained by a critical assumption: subjects are captured at close range, typically under one meter. No existing benchmark systematically addresses multi-distance capture, diverse environmental conditions, and concurrent spoofing and occlusion-based attacks, leaving deployed models underprepared for real-world scenarios. We introduce a video-based PAD dataset of 374,000+ frames from 261 unique identities collected across five standoff distances (1 m-100 m) under indoor and outdoor conditions using a DSLR camera (C) and a mobile sensor (M), with three-class labels: live, spoof, and props (occlusions); models are trained and evaluated on video clips rather than single frames. We fine-tune and benchmark four CNN architectures: MobileNetV3, MobileNet, EfficientNet, and ResNet-50. The higher-resolution DSLR maintains near-perfect spoof classification rate across all distances, while the lower-resolution mobile sensor degrades sharply beyond 50 m, with props classification rate dropping to 55% at 75 m for MobileNetV3. EfficientNet achieves the best overall performance (98.48% accuracy, ACER 2.01%). Generalization tests on unseen attack datasets yield 89-94% accuracy, validating cross-domain robustness. These results establish capture distance and sensor resolution as critical but underexplored axes of PAD difficulty. The dataset will be publicly released under an End-User License Agreement to support reproducible long-range PAD research.

items.title: Fast and Memory-Light Evaluation of Density-Based Clusterings with the DISCO Index in R
items.description: arXiv:2611.25114v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: DISCO is a recent internal cluster validity index for density-based clustering that, unlike earlier indices, also evaluates the quality of noise labels. The discoCVI package makes DISCO available in R. This article describes the design of the package and a typical workflow, in which DISCO is used to compare clusterings and to choose the parameters of HDBSCAN without ground truth, followed by the implementation introduced in version 0.2.0. DISCO is defined through density-connectivity distances between all pairs of points, so direct implementations store several n-by-n matrices. We show that every quantity DISCO needs can be read off the single-linkage merge tree of the mutual-reachability minimum spanning tree, so that the index can be computed exactly with memory that grows linearly with the number of points, while the running time remains quadratic as in the original definition. The implementation is tested against the previous version, agrees with the original Python implementation to within $3 \times 10^{-13}$, and corrects the score of singleton clusters to match the published definition. In benchmarks, discoCVI is 23 to 138 times faster than its previous version for 500 to 4,000 points and 3 to 9 times faster than the Python reference for 500 to 8,000 points, using a fraction of the memory of both, and it scores 100,000 points in about 50 seconds with less than 200 MB of memory.

items.title: Auditing Learned Dynamics in Weather Models
items.description: arXiv:2611.25119v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learned weather models are experimentally accessible computational systems whose internal representations can be inspected and manipulated. Using sparse autoencoder features from GraphCast, DeepMind's autoregressive weather forecasting model, we test whether causal relevance requires physical semantics, a question that matters for auditing whether AI forecasters used in high-assurance settings rely on reliable mechanisms. We also look at whether physically associated latent directions can be steered to improve extreme-event forecasts, where interventions are applied to the model's internal activations during the rollout. We find that ablating a feature locked to GraphCast's computational mesh increases global geopotential height error despite lacking conventional physical semantics. Second, suppressing convection- and low-level-vorticity-associated features weakens predicted tropical-cyclone deepening (the fall in central pressure during intensification), while amplifying them reduces intensity error, with amplification of convection features through feature scaling achieving a median of 51\% error reduction over seven storms. Together, these results separate interpretable, physical association from causal utility and establish sparse features as experimental coordinates for auditing and intervening on learned weather dynamics.

items.title: Temporal Extrapolation of Elastic Seismic Wave Propagation in Layered Media Using Neural Operators
items.description: arXiv:2611.25130v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal prediction of seismic velocity fields beyond the time interval represented in training remains challenging for neural operator models. This study develops a coupled neural operator framework for stress-conditioned temporal prediction in layered elastic media. A time-integrator-embedded Deep Operator Network (TI-DeepONet) advances the velocity field through an embedded fourth-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) scheme, while a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) learns a residual correction to the predicted spatial field. The two components are trained jointly in a predictor-corrector configuration. Prediction is initialized with reference velocity fields at the first two time levels and proceeds autoregressively, with reference stress fields and prescribed excitation supplied throughout rollout, including beyond the training interval. Four cases consider horizontally polarized shear (SH) waves in four-layer soil columns with fixed total depths of 50 and 280 m, excited by third-order Gaussian-derivative (DOG3) wavelets with central frequencies between 0.5 and 6 Hz. Layer thicknesses and shear-wave velocities vary across profiles. Evaluations on test profiles extend beyond the training interval by up to twice its duration. The predictions reproduce principal velocity arrivals and depth-dependent response patterns, with accuracy varying across profiles. Across the four cases, mean peak-normalized root-mean-square errors (NRMSEs) range from 0.53% to 2.31% over the full evaluation windows and from 0.61% to 2.82% over the extrapolation intervals. Both metrics use each profile's peak absolute reference velocity over the full evaluation window as the normalizer. These results demonstrate temporal velocity prediction under reference-stress conditioning for the tested configurations; autonomous continuation of the coupled velocity-stress wavefield remains to be established.

items.title: Rate-distortion Assessment for Hierarchical Content Summarization
items.description: arXiv:2611.25151v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Powerful generative models including large language and vision models have demonstrated success across a wide range of content generation, editing and manipulation tasks via end-to-end prompt-based generation. However, current assessment of the quality of generative content manipulation remains subjective, limiting scientific understanding of model capabilities. Inspired by rate-distortion theory from Shannon information compression theory, in this work we formalize hierarchical content summarization as an information encoding problem. We design a principled framework to extract the semantic hierarchy of the source content to support quantitative characterization of the rate-distortion trade-off between compression efficiency (rate) against information loss (distortion) during generative content manipulation, which allows us to benchmark various models with respect to performance conditional on rate budget of interest. We demonstrate the use of the framework with empirical experiments on content summarization for long-context question-answering with state-of-the-art large language models, offering new insights into their efficiency and comprehension capabilities. We further demonstrate the use of the semantic hierarchy as guidance for performing effective retrieval augmented generation, showing improved rate-distortion characteristics against current baselines.

items.title: Bayesian $\kappa$-Explorer for Minimax Model Estimation in MDPs
items.description: arXiv:2611.25160v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study active exploration for minimax transition estimation in unknown Markov decision processes (MDPs). Frequentist $\kappa$-Explorer~\citep{gu2026kappa} addresses this problem through a parameterized family of exploration objectives, but requires confidence-bound constructions and joint optimization over plausible transition kernels and occupancy measures, introducing a computational burden that limits its practical applicability. We develop Bayesian $\kappa$-Explorer, which simplifies this procedure by placing Dirichlet priors on the transition distributions. Under the posterior mean estimator, the posterior expected squared $\ell_2$ error equals the total posterior variance, providing a closed-form exploration signal. The algorithm plans under the posterior mean model, eliminating confidence-set optimization. Under the stated assumptions, this simpler planning procedure retains the $\widetilde{O}(T^{-1/3})$ surrogate convergence rate of frequentist $\kappa$-Explorer. We further bound the maximum posterior variance relative to the optimal asymptotic minimax allocation benchmark. Experiments on Pendulum, Mountain Car, and Taxi demonstrate lower worst-case transition-estimation errors than the tested baselines.

items.title: Separating Interpretability and Reconstruction in Sparse Autoencoders
items.description: arXiv:2611.25165v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are effective tools for mechanistic interpretability by decomposing neural representations into sparse and interpretable features. However, a single sparse representation in traditional SAEs is responsible for both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability, which are not guaranteed to align. To separate these objectives, we propose DualSAE, a modular framework that augments standard SAEs with a plug-in Residual Branch. A standard SAE serves as the Sparse Branch, learning a sparse code that contains the dominant semantics of the input. The added Residual Branch models the non-semantic information omitted by the Sparse Branch. We ensure that the contributions of the two branches towards the overall reconstruction have minimal overlap through a decorrelation loss. We also adopt a two-stage training strategy that first stabilizes sparse representation learning before coupling with the Residual Branch. Across diverse encoder-SAE configurations on two vision datasets and two language corpora, DualSAE achieves mean relative improvements of approximately 29% in reconstruction fidelity and 34% in interpretability (measured by monosemanticity score). Moreover, with more interpretable representations, DualSAE yields consistent performance gains in the downstream applications of topic modeling, hypothesis generation, and LLM steering. Qualitative analysis further suggests that the Sparse Branch indeed preserves dominant semantic content, whereas the Residual Branch captures non-semantic information to improve reconstruction fidelity.

items.title: PDE-State Conditioning for Learned Optimization Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks
items.description: arXiv:2611.25185v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) optimization depends on global properties of the underlying PDE and how the physics residual evolves across the domain. Standard optimizers such as Adam use fixed gradient-based statistics, while learned PINN optimizers replace the fixed rule with a learned update built from local parameters and optimization-history features. However, none explicitly use PDE-level information. We study two coupled design questions: what PDE-level information should a learned optimizer observe, and how should that information influence its update? We introduce an 11-dimensional PDE state-capturing operator structure, residual geometry, and short-horizon update response, and use it to condition a structured meta-learned optimizer through bounded feature-wise modulation. Repeated design studies identify the compact residual-geometry state G2 and bounded FiLM as the strongest overall choices among those tested. The resulting PDE-State-conditioned optimizer improves all evaluation metrics (relative-L2, L1, solution MSE, and physics MSE) over Adam and the unconditioned learned optimizer on Linear Advection, KdV, and Burgers.

items.title: {\phi}TD: Distributional Reinforcement Learning using Characteristic Functions
items.description: arXiv:2611.25208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributional Reinforcement Learning methods aim to learn the entire distribution of returns, yet current algorithmic approaches are limited to a narrow class of distributions. We propose $\varphi$TD, a method to overcome this limitation by computing the loss in the frequency domain. We demonstrate that this further unifies quantile and categorical approaches to distributional RL, and enables the learning of distributions that were previously impossible to capture, such as mixtures of continuous distributions. We empirically study $\varphi$TD, across synthetic benchmarks and large-scale deep RL environments and demonstrate that the flexibility obtained from wider parametric families can lead to improved performance.

items.title: Some Memories Must Fade: Persistence and Decay of User Memories in Model Parameters
items.description: arXiv:2611.25235v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parametric memory allows Large Language Models to internalize knowledge directly into their weights, offering a potentially powerful alternative to retrieval-based memory (RAG). However, existing approaches to parametric memory are difficult to deploy as they largely mirror the Continual Learning (CL) objective of retaining information indefinitely. This is neither sustainable nor sufficient for a memory system, which must govern knowledge across its lifecycle by retaining stable facts, reinforcing recurring observations, updating changed beliefs, and allowing transient information to fade. We propose a system for parametric memory management consisting of a memory substrate (handling information storage and forgetting) and a learned policy (what to remember, how deeply, and for how long). Our substrate is a fixed-capacity LoRA adapter that consists of k-hot rank combinations which store facts without catastrophic interference and maintain an independently controlled temporal decay, enabling outdated information to fade while long-term facts persist. On this substrate, we train a lightweight controller that governs each incoming user event to ensure the memory system reflects the user's true, updated belief state. To evaluate how memory systems manage user memory, we introduce a controlled dataset of long-horizon user trajectories with varying persistence of facts based on changing belief states and user-behavioral shifts, and probe queries that test recall while information is valid and abstention after it expires. Our policy learns to effectively manage user memory over its entire lifecycle, balancing recall and abstention to achieve 86% of oracle performance, unlike CL and RAG baselines that primarily default to one of the two behaviors. By providing the first system to manage memory directly in model weights, this work establishes a foundation for long-horizon parametric memory.

items.title: Moving Generality from Model to Modeler: LLM Agents for PHM on a Deployment-Style Benchmark
items.description: arXiv:2611.25252v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents built on large language models (LLMs) now help develop many models published as general solutions. Should generality instead reside in the agent that builds a model for each new task? We examine this question in prognostics and health management (PHM), where every model must work on unseen equipment. Our deployment-style benchmark, NextUnit-Bench, covers 24 public datasets split into 58 folds that hold out units or operating conditions; each agent has two hours to deliver an executable predictor, then run on the hidden units. First, frontier agents outperform AutoML, which reaches less than half the best agent's score, and faithful implementations of published methods on four datasets, of which only 6 of 30 beat the strongest agent's own design; published accuracies, where reproducible, rest on the papers' own conventions, and a single convention, capping the remaining life of test engines, can halve the reported error. Second, the agents' advantage is a design made on each machine's data; once made, a plain-text plan of a few hundred words carries most of the gap between two frontier agents, and given a weaker agent's plan, the strongest agent falls to that agent's level, often to identical predictions. Before touching the data, however, it matters little whose plan an agent carries out, and domain toolkits appear to help neither: what sets the strongest apart is how much it learns from the data. Third, such designs reach only implementers that can execute them: given the strongest agent's designs, a locally deployable open-weight model delivers half as often, even when they are lightened, and scores no higher than without them. Generality, we argue, is not disappearing but moving, from the model to the modeler.

items.title: Process-Knowledge-Guided Latent Diffusion for Generative Design of Porous Architectures: A Case Study in Aerosol Jet Printing
items.description: arXiv:2611.25264v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Printed porous layouts interleave functional material with open channels, and the layout that uses the material best depends on how the process settings shape the deposit. Generative models propose layouts quickly, but a generator that does not receive the process setting samples from the same distribution at every setting, even when the process-dependent score ranks candidate layouts differently. This paper examines whether process knowledge can steer a latent diffusion generator toward layouts suited to a given process setting in a prescribed design domain. We formulate a process-dependent utilization score in which a process model sets the length over which the utility of printed material decays with distance from a channel. The generator combines a vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) latent representation, a topology U-Net, a ControlNet domain branch, and a separately trained regressor that predicts the score from noised latents; the domain branch conditions each denoising step and the regressor gradient steers it. The method is applied to aerosol jet printing, where the atomizer and sheath gas flows enter the score through the flow-focusing relation. Across seven modeled flow settings, the lowest-scoring candidate layout of a domain differed between settings in 191 of 500 domains. In a sampling study, the mean directly computed score on three validation domains and one test domain was 0.642 with domain conditioning alone, 0.636 at a weight of 300, and 0.450 at 12,000 (112 scores per weight; lower is better). The results support process-knowledge-guided generation as an approach to process-specific porous design under the stated assumptions.

items.title: Learning to Verify: Signature-Guided Training for Adaptive Adversarial Detection
items.description: arXiv:2611.25271v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adversarial example detectors often fail when attackers explicitly attempt to bypass them. We propose a dual-model approach that keeps the original classifier fixed and trains a separate verifier to assess its predictions. During training, we identify patterns of internal neural network activations that distinguish genuine examples of each class from adversarial examples targeting that class. These patterns, called activation signatures, guide the generation of challenging adversarial examples that mislead the classifier, challenge the verifier, and internally resemble the target class. The verifier learns to recognize these examples while preserving its performance on clean inputs through knowledge distillation. At inference, the verifier evaluates the classifier's prediction without requiring activation signatures. We evaluate the approach on publicly available datasets against several adaptive attacks, including attacks unseen during training. The proposed verifier substantially outperforms directly attacked confidence-based and feature-based detectors under the evaluated L-infinity attacks. Ablation studies show that adaptive verifier training is the main source of this improvement, while signature guidance primarily benefits clean accuracy. Additional L2 evaluations reveal limitations in robustness across perturbation types.

items.title: Scone: Symmetry-aware Neural Combinatorial Optimization for Graph Coloring
items.description: arXiv:2611.25273v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph coloring, which entails assigning colors to nodes such that no adjacent nodes have the same color, is a fundamental combinatorial optimization problem. In general, however, finding a node coloring with no monochromatic edges given a fixed palette is NP-hard. This motivates learning-based methods that can learn to exploit recurring structure across instances to efficiently produce high-quality colorings. Crucially, the validity of a coloring is invariant to permutations of the colors, and we show that exploiting this symmetry reduces the size of the effective state space over which the model has to learn its policy. At the same time, the coloring algorithm must be able to break some symmetries, for example to assign different colors to two adjacent nodes belonging to the same automorphism orbit. In this paper, we introduce Scone, a model that uses a color-equivariant graph neural network to construct colorings sequentially, allowing information from previous assignments to propagate and break node symmetries. Scone achieves perfect solution quality with low inference times across several graph coloring tasks, including on sudoku_extreme and register allocations, and showcases generalization to graph families not encountered during training.

items.title: DS3M: Deep structured state space models for nonlinear system identification on modern hardware
items.description: arXiv:2611.25274v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural state-space identification learns dynamical models from measured inputs and outputs. SUBNET combines this task with an encoder that estimates initial states from short measurement histories. Its continuous-time version requires many successive neural-network evaluations during numerical integration, resulting in slow training speed which is a major limitation for practical use cases. We propose deep structured state space models (DS3M), which combine compact nonlinear dynamical components in parallel and in series. Custom GPU kernels implemented with Triton reduce the launch and memory overhead of their sequential evaluation. We explain this construction, describe a port-Hamiltonian variant, and present various benchmark comparisons of accuracy and training time.

items.title: Intelligent Embedding Pruning for Large-Scale Recommendation Models
items.description: arXiv:2611.25288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern recommendation systems face substantial memory pressure, largely from the sparse embedding layer that maps high-cardinality categorical features into dense vectors. In-training embedding pruning (ITEP) removes less important embedding rows during training, yielding end-to-end memory savings but sometimes degrading accuracy because per-table pruning ratios are set by size-based heuristics. We use feature importance (FI) to guide these ratios (FI-ITEP), assigning higher pruning to tables tied to less important features. Across three large-scale recommendation models, FI-ITEP achieves 20--40% total memory reduction while matching or improving accuracy relative to percentile-based ITEP. Because the feature-importance signal requires minimal resources to compute, these memory savings translate into concrete systems benefits: the same models train on fewer GPU trainers (e.g., 112 to 80) with higher per-GPU throughput, saving 1,000+ GPU-hours per model launch. We reproduce these trends on the open-source DLRM (Criteo 1TB) and quantify the end-to-end training-time and GPU-cost tradeoff---including the burden of computing FI---offering practical guidance for embedding pruning in real-world systems.

items.title: Cross-Question Reliable Reinforcement Learning
items.description: arXiv:2611.25292v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI systems operating near the limits of their capabilities can maximize utility while minimizing the risk of error by abstaining or deferring questions they are not confident about to a human or a stronger model. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have been post-trained to estimate confidence in their own answers. To achieve this, methods reinforce confidence scores based on the correctness signal to each question-answer pair individually, with rewards that encourage assigning confidence 1 to correct answers and 0 to incorrect answers. However, estimating confidence scores is useful in that it enables selecting only the most confident answers, to maximize the share of solved questions while accommodating the user's risk tolerance. Assigning confidence 1 to correct answers and 0 to incorrect ones is theoretically optimal, but unattainable in practice and detrimental for selective prediction with a non-zero risk tolerance: confidences pushed to 0 and 1 carry no information about how answers compare to one another. We therefore introduce CARE (Cross-question Abstention Reward Estimation), which computes rewards over a set of question-answer pairs: At each of several risk tolerances, the confidences across the set induce an abstention threshold, and each confidence is rewarded for lying on the correct side of it. Since the threshold itself comes from the set, every verbalized confidence is reinforced relative to other questions' confidence, not against its own binary correctness label. On math, CARE increases the coverage at 5% risk (C@5) across MATH-500, GSM8K, and Big-Math-Digits from 0.8% to 42.4%, compared to existing pointwise correctness-matching rewards. When trained on multi-hop Wikipedia QA from HotpotQA, CARE improves C@5 in out-of-distribution general-knowledge, reasoning, and math benchmarks (including CommonsenseQA, GPQA, SimpleQA, and TriviaQA) from 12.3% to 23.6%.

items.title: Federated Learning of Car Aerodynamics Surrogates with Spectral Optimizers
items.description: arXiv:2611.25300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural surrogates predict the aerodynamic forces on a car in seconds, compared with hours for a CFD simulation, but training them requires thousands of CFD simulations of different car designs, which car manufacturers keep proprietary. Federated learning allows several manufacturers to train a shared surrogate without exchanging data. We study which federated optimizer brings such a surrogate closest to one trained on pooled data. On DrivAerNet++, we train a Transolver surrogate across six clients that each hold cars of a single body type, and we compare three spectral optimizers, which orthogonalize the update of each weight matrix (FedMuon and two methods we propose, FedMARS-M and FedOLion), with three non-spectral ones (FedAvg, SCAFFOLD-Adam and FedLion), all tuned with the same protocol. FedMuon and FedMARS-M reach a drag error within 2% of centralized training with Muon, using two to four local epochs per round. The non-spectral methods perform best with sixteen local epochs, the largest number we tested, and still have a 17 to 37% higher drag error than FedMARS-M. We relate this gap to the low stable rank of the weight gradients, for which an orthogonalized step yields about twice the first-order decrease of a gradient step of the same spectral norm. Code: https://github.com/armanbolatov/fedmars_drivaernet

items.title: SplitReAlign: Partition-Aware Representation Realignment for Split Federated Unlearning
items.description: arXiv:2611.25301v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Split federated learning (SFL) distributes neural networks across clients and a server, coupling class-specific knowledge across their representations. This coupling complicates split federated unlearning (SFU), where class-wise forgetting must remove target knowledge while preserving retained utility under heterogeneous representation spaces and asymmetric update constraints. We propose SplitReAlign, a partition-aware representation realignment framework for class-wise SFU. It constructs endpoint-specific discriminative subspaces coordinated through a shared semantic anchor, selectively realigning forgotten representations while penalizing changes outside the active subspaces. To accommodate asymmetric update constraints, SplitReAlign leverages gradients through frozen servers for Client-only updates and fixed client-feature statistics for Server-only guidance, while Joint updates optimize both partitions. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 under heterogeneous client distributions demonstrate that SplitReAlign achieves the lowest average gap to retraining among all compared methods across six settings. Notably, Server-only achieves the closest agreement with retraining on both datasets, highlighting the effectiveness of partition-aware guidance under restricted updates.

items.title: When Is Program Structure Required? Certificate-Grounded Calibration of Program-Induction Difficulty
items.description: arXiv:2611.24975v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A program-induction benchmark is informative when its examples require the structure it aims to test. Yet a two-rule generator can produce demonstrations that a single rule also explains. We introduce certificate-grounded calibration, which constructs matched tasks with minimum solution lengths of one and two in a bounded string-replacement language. Complete one-rule enumeration and an executable two-rule witness certify the change before model inference. We evaluate 120 reference families with three to six shared examples, using 1,440 new model trajectories and 480 saved trajectories. Across Qwen3-8B and Olmo-3-7B-Think, displayed-task completion is 23.53-45.83 percentage points lower on certified separation tasks, while success on a wholly unshown witness pair is 8.40-13.45 points higher. These witness gains accompany lower agreement on uniformly sampled strings and 1.93-5.78% agreement on inputs that activate both reference rules. Recertification also reveals that a single unchanged example can exclude a shortcut and determine whether two rules are required. Together, these results show how the evidence supplied by examples shapes both the required solution and the programs models produce. The construction provides an executable testbed for comparing program search, final-answer delivery, and behavior on new inputs under verified task requirements.

items.title: Improving On-board Shape Models Using Sun Sensors and Implicit Representations
items.description: arXiv:2611.24976v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose an original, end-to-end approach to generate and refine the onboard 3D shape model of irregular small bodies, such as asteroids, using only low-cost Sun sensor eclipse data and coarse a priori knowledge, tailored for resource-constrained missions like CubeSats. Leveraging EclipseNets, a differentiable neural model of eclipse boundaries, our pipeline first refines 2D silhouettes by learning from real-time entry and exit events during spacecraft orbits, avoiding the limitations of traditional imaging or lidar in bandwidth-starved environments. These silhouettes then supervise a compact neural signed-distance field with periodic activations, enabling incremental updates to a high-fidelity implicit geometry representation capable of capturing fine-scale features and concavities. In simulations of the body Eros under realistic orbital dynamics, the method increases silhouette IoU from 0.70 to 0.87 and produces coherent 3D reconstructions, suggesting our approach could find a place in future autonomous architectures for small-body exploration.

items.title: DL101 The Representation Capability of Neural Network Models
items.description: arXiv:2611.24980v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Universal approximation theorems (Cybenko, Funahashi, Hornik & Leshno) provide the mathematical justification for why neural networks are powerful enough to model complex, nonlinear phenomena. Shallow networks can approximate any continuous function on compact sets. Leshno's theorem clarified that non-polynomial activations are necessary for universality, which explains why ReLU, logistic, hyperbolic tangent, and other common activations work (but pure polynomials do not). However, approximation theorems provide no efficiency, training, nor generalization guarantees. They do not indicate how many neurons are needed for a given accuracy, whether gradient descent will find the right parameters, or whether networks trained on finite data will generalize well. Barron provided quantitative error bounds for particular function classes (approximation rates for functions with bounded Fourier norm), whereas Mont\'ufar was the first to show that expressivity grows exponentially with depth (in terms of the number of linear regions). Deep networks are strictly more expressive than shallow ones with the same number of parameters. Depth is fundamentally more powerful than width, providing a rigorous mathematical explanation for the use of deep learning models.

items.title: Risk-optimal active learning with informative abstention
items.description: arXiv:2611.24986v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study label acquisition when an oracle may abstain and its response probability shares parameters with the classifier. A query can then provide information through both a returned label and the response outcome. Under a correctly specified parametric model, we derive the classifier information after adjustment for response-model nuisance parameters. Combining this information with the local curvature of multiclass zero-one risk gives an acquisition criterion for minimizing the leading asymptotic excess risk. We characterize the optimal allocation under a fixed query budget and show how query allocation affects response identifiability. The oracle criterion reduces to response-discounted acquisition when response probability does not depend on the classifier parameters. Simulations examine the resulting query allocations and isolate the contribution of the response-outcome term through an ablation. A Consumer Complaints replay retains observed human abstentions and reveals benchmark labels upon response. Response-aware acquisition has lower mean test error than response-discounted acquisition at the two largest budgets, with paired differences significant after Holm correction. Entropy sampling performs better at the smallest budget. The gains depend on the response mechanism and query budget.

items.title: Variance-Adaptive Upper Confidence Bounds for Multi-Armed Bandits with Kaplan--Meier Survival Estimation
items.description: arXiv:2611.24988v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the stochastic multi-armed bandit problem in which the reward associated with each arm is the survival probability at a pre-specified time horizon, and the observed outcome is a right-censored time-to-event variable. Standard bandit algorithms face delayed and partial observations in this setting. Prior adaptations for the Kaplan--Meier (KM) estimator rely on Hoeffding-type bounds that ignore the inherent heteroscedasticity of continuous survival processes. To bridge this gap, we propose KM-UCB, a variance-adaptive policy that unites continuous-time survival analysis with discrete sequential decision-making. By leveraging martingale theory and continuous influence functions, we derive a fixed-cohort empirical Bernstein bound parameterized by Greenwood's variance formula. For realtime allocation, we retain the Greenwood index and use a survival bound from completed records to review the recommended arm. Under catch-up reporting, the policy has logarithmic expected regret with an arm-specific variance term in the exploration bound. We evaluate the original policy in a dual-layer delayed simulation and a retrospective replay of breast cancer trial data, and evaluate the correction in a separate paired simulation.

items.title: Infer3D: Inverse Generative Modeling Enables Robust 3D Reconstruction
items.description: arXiv:2611.25061v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Humans can understand the 3D structure of scenes even from highly unfamiliar or extreme viewpoints. Cognitive science suggests this generalization stems from a top-down generative inference strategy. In contrast, state-of-the-art 3D reconstruction neural networks typically rely on amortized, feedforward inference. While fast, this pattern-matching approach degrades when faced with out-of-distribution (OOD) scene conditions unseen during training. Inspired by the generative nature of human vision, we propose Infer3D, an inverse generative modeling framework that recovers the latent variables of a generative model to best match the monocular input. To prevent degenerate flat outputs, we couple the generative image prior with a frozen 3D lifting network that constrains the optimization space to a valid, multi-view-consistent 3D manifold. Across a variety of controlled synthetic and real-world tasks, Infer3D demonstrates superior OOD reconstruction accuracy compared to feedforward networks trained on equal or larger datasets. Furthermore, mirroring how human perception requires more time to process confusing stimuli, we introduce an adaptive inference strategy that expends more test-time compute on ambiguous OOD examples while efficiently routing in-distribution inputs. Project website: https://amanikiruga.github.io/infer3d-site/

items.title: Empirical Variational Bayes Factorization for Longitudinal Matrix Data
items.description: arXiv:2611.25065v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Collecting high-dimensional data over time for multiple individuals is increasingly common in biomedical research, particularly in studies of disease progression or molecular time-course experiments. Often data are missing or the timepoints are irregularly spaced across individuals. There is a lack of flexible methodology to explore latent patterns of change over time and account for missing data. We propose an empirical variational Bayes (EVB) approach to factorize high-dimensional longitudinal data, in which the underlying factors have temporal correlation over time. The EVB approach is computationally efficient and accommodates flexible covariance structures over time with automatic determination of all hyper-parameters (including the underlying rank, i.e., number of factors). Simulations demonstrate that the approach captures the underlying signal more precisely than other strategies, and performs well with respect to missing data imputation under different scenarios. An application to a gene time-course data for multiple sclerosis treatment provides a factorization with interpretable components over time and improved imputation accuracy for missing data.

items.title: PriTabICL: Differentially Private Tabular In-Context Learning with Task-Aligned Cluster-Wise Synthesis
items.description: arXiv:2611.25073v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tabular in-context learning (TabICL) enables large language models (LLMs) to predict target records using a handful of labeled demonstrations in their prompts. However, these demonstrations often contain sensitive personal information. Differential privacy (DP) offers principled protection, but noise-based methods introduce substantial noise, distorting the feature-label relationships essential for accurate prediction, especially as data dimensionality grows. In this work, we study DP data synthesis for generating privacy-preserving TabICL demonstrations. We identify two limitations of directly applying general-purpose DP synthesis to entire datasets: modeling a global distribution can obscure local structure and minority patterns in heterogeneous data, while measuring broad attribute dependencies under a limited privacy budget can reduce the accuracy available for relationships most relevant to prediction. More broadly, global statistical fidelity may fail to preserve heterogeneous structures needed by downstream predictive and generative models. To address these challenges, we propose PriTabICL, a general framework compatible with existing DP synthesis algorithms. It partitions records into DP clusters and synthesizes each independently, using a fixed feature-target workload to prioritize prediction-relevant statistical relationships. At inference, each query is routed to a DP cluster, and demonstrations are sampled from its synthetic dataset without additional privacy loss for the original records. Experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods across heterogeneous datasets. In particular, one of our instantiations, PriTabICL-PrivSyn, improves over global PrivSyn in 8 out of 12 settings and outperforms existing private TabICL approaches in nearly all evaluated settings. Open-source code is available.

items.title: BuggyMLE: Scaling Machine Learning Engineering Difficulty with Bug Injection
items.description: arXiv:2611.25088v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Enabling AI systems to autonomously improve AI models requires agents capable of performing machine learning engineering (MLE). In practice, designing, training, and evaluating complex models demands modifying multi-file repositories to reproduce results, debug training runs, integrate datasets, and port frameworks. However, existing MLE benchmarks limit agents to single-file edits without full repository or shell access, and common repository-level software engineering benchmarks have rapidly saturated. To address this, we introduce the Code Complexity Index (CCI), a difficulty metric based on ten structural features spanning repository scale, dependency depth, and patch size. CCI strongly predicts average solve rates across eight public coding benchmarks ($R^2 = 0.951$), identifying patch size and complexity as top predictors. Guided by CCI, we develop BuggyMLE, a scalable framework where agents inject controlled mutations into working ML repositories, synthesizing over 6,600 bug-injected MLE repository variants and nearly 260K lines of injected code based on 222 source repositories. Using BuggyMLE, we make two contributions. First, we construct BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite, the first difficulty-graded, repository-level variant of MLE-Bench Lite; across 14 evaluated models, the top solve rate drops from 95% to 9% as difficulty is scaled from the easiest to the hardest tier. Second, we synthesize a training curriculum across three difficulty levels over 200 additional ML repositories, fine-tuning a Qwen3.5-9B model to rival frontier models on BuggyMLE-Bench-Lite. Our trained model transfers beyond ML, raising its SWE-bench Lite resolve rate from 24% to 33% and its LiveCodeBench v6 pass@1 from 69% to 71%.

items.title: CAIMS: Scalable Cross-Array In-Memory Search
items.description: arXiv:2611.25141v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Search, especially top-k similarity search, plays a vital role in many applications, but its performance can be severely limited by memory access overhead. In-memory search (IMS), an alternative to CPU/GPU-based approaches, exploits massive parallelism within a content-addressable memory (CAM) array to perform search in situ and provides both low latency and high energy efficiency. However, the capacity of a single CAM array is often insufficient for modern workloads, requiring data to be distributed across multiple arrays. Deploying scalable top-k similarity search across multiple CAM arrays poses a fundamental problem that existing designs fail to address: how to accurately and efficiently reduce local binary match results to global top-k results. This work introduces CAIMS, a cross-array IMS framework that is agnostic to memory technologies and applications, enabling scalable and efficient top-k similarity search while preserving accuracy. To enable accurate top-k result reduction, CAIMS leverages the existing threshold match functionality with a combined offline and online parameter selection approach to transform local binary match results that lack globally comparable similarity information into global coarse-grained similarity scores. To further improve efficiency, CAIMS conducts hierarchical reduction and transfers only the selection results and necessary control signals with lightweight local peripherals. Implemented on a 3D NAND Flash model and demonstrated using the retrieval phase of retrieval-augmented generation, CAIMS improves throughput by up to $22.3\times/10.1\times$ and energy efficiency by $426.6\times/23.7\times$ compared to the server-class CPU baseline and prior 3D NAND Flash accelerators, respectively, while maintaining comparable accuracy.

items.title: Before the Choice: An Evidential Framework for Studying Prospective Representations in Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2611.25170v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: An observable decision reveals the selected action but does not determine which alternatives were internally represented. Drawing on prospection research and hippocampal forward-sweep observations, we develop Before the Choice, an evidence-oriented framework distinguishing future-directed content, prospective computation, and causal guidance. The framework organizes four experimental contrasts and makes their alternative explanations explicit. Its first test case concerns unchosen trajectories in deterministic symbolic environments. A preregistered low-rank probe evaluated once on a sealed TEST did not meet its criterion (paired accuracy 0.020 versus 0.195 for a text-and-observed-choice baseline; 293 admissible pairs). Exploratory H1b exposed a reconstruction-by-elimination problem: identifying the chosen candidate can determine the unchosen target. In H1c, matched worlds varied an unchosen continuation while keeping candidate keys bitwise invariant. With specified positive controls passed, decoding in the late-key condition remained at 0.521 (p = 0.18; 141 contributing families). These observations do not identify prospective simulation or establish an absence of prospective representations. They illustrate why identifiability, sensitivity, and a dependence-aware null model must constrain inferences from decodability. PREM is proposed as an organizational framework and is not validated by these results. We offer it as a methodological contribution to empirical AI welfare research, which will require such evidential distinctions. Code and protocol records: https://github.com/besionisrael/before-choice

items.title: MADJEPA: Enhanced Multi-Stage Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for Medical Anomaly Detection
items.description: arXiv:2611.25194v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Anomaly detection in medical images is a complex task, requiring the development of a robust model using only healthy patient data. Without access to labeled data, modern approaches typically employ self-supervised learning to obtain a model of normality. Since world models promise to build strong internal representations of their environment, we consider them as suitable candidates for the medical anomaly detection environment, namely medical investigations of healthy patients. To this end, we propose MADJEPA, a medical anomaly detector based on an enhanced multi-stage joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA). We design a multi-stage training pipeline to produce a robust detector: (1) image-based JEPA (I-JEPA) training aims to learn a strong representation of normal training data; (2) target encoder distillation aims to modulate over-generalization of I-JEPA representations to abnormal data; (3) pseudo-anomaly classification aims to calibrate anomaly predictions by learning a tight boundary around the normal data manifold. To demonstrate our design, we carry out comprehensive experiments on six datasets covering various medical image domains (e.g.~MRI, OCT, X-ray, histopathology), comparing our MADJEPA with numerous state-of-the-art methods. The results show that our carefully designed world model, MADJEPA, attains competitive results, ranking first on three datasets. Our ablation studies further confirm the utility of each training stage, indicating that I-JEPA alone is not sufficient to obtain competitive results in medical anomaly detection. We publicly release our code at https://github.com/Sabina085/madjepa.

items.title: From Self-Play RL to Constrained Control: Distilling DiffMPC Students with DAgger
items.description: arXiv:2611.25197v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Self-play reinforcement learning (RL) produces strong driving policies, but these policies are hard to verify or interpret. Differentiable model predictive control (DiffMPC) can enforce explicit constraints, but it is usually trained by imitating logged data or with costly RL. To add constraints to an already trained policy, we keep a PPO teacher's backbone and replace its action head with a DiffMPC that enforces road boundary half-planes and agent ellipses. We then distill the student with DAgger in the teacher's self-play simulator. Over 9 seeds, the constrained student of a smaller teacher matches its teacher on nuPlan and beats it on CARLA and on out-of-distribution Waymo scenes. For a stronger teacher, the student has fewer failures on nuPlan and Waymo, while staying level on CARLA. Its distillation takes no more than 30% of the teacher's training time.

items.title: Statistical, Machine Learning and Deep Learning Methods for Missing Covariates: An Empirical Evaluation with Applications to Alzheimer's Disease Research
items.description: arXiv:2611.25219v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Missing data are common in biomedical research, particularly when biomarkers are costly or require invasive procedures to obtain, such as cerebrospinal fluid measures in Alzheimer's disease. Although a wide range of missing data methods exists, from traditional statistical approaches to modern machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms, their comparative performance under different missingness mechanisms remains insufficiently understood. In this study, we provide an empirical evaluation of eight methods for handling missing covariates, including complete-case analysis, multiple imputation, ML-based techniques, and DL frameworks such as multilayer perceptrons, variational autoencoders, and generative adversarial networks. We summarize their conceptual foundations, practical implementation considerations, strengths, and limitations. Through extensive simulations, we assess estimation bias, efficiency, standard error accuracy, confidence interval coverage, and computational burden across different missingness mechanisms and proportions. An application to the Vanderbilt Memory and Aging Project further illustrates the implications of different methods for regression analysis in a real-world biomedical setting. Finally, we provide practical recommendations for method selection and highlight remaining challenges that warrant future investigation.

items.title: Stability Bands for Feature Attribution: The Core, the Nucleolus and the Bargaining Set of Explained-Variance Games
items.description: arXiv:2611.25238v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Shapley-value attributions are the default way of explaining machine-learning predictions in economics, but they report a single number per feature and say nothing about whether a coalition of features that jointly accounts for more than it receives could contest that allocation. We study feature attribution through the core, the nucleolus and the bargaining set of an explained-variance game, in which the worth of a set of features is the variance of the model's predictions that those features generate. For every feature we report a stability band (its range of shares over the core, or over the least core when the core is empty), with the nucleolus as distinguished point and a certificate that the allocation admits no justified objection. Three results organise the approach. First, for linear models the game is exactly 2-additive, with pairwise Harsanyi dividends $2\beta_i\beta_j\sigma_{ij}$, so multicollinearity is what creates coalitional structure. Second, in every 2-additive game the prenucleolus coincides with the Shapley value, the (least) core is point-symmetric around it, and the core is non-empty if and only if every cut of the interaction graph has non-negative weight. The Shapley value thus always lies in the prebargaining set, and stability adds information only through band widths and interactions of order three or more. Third, for convex games the bands have a closed form and any allocation can be certified with one minimum cut. In a hedonic price model, the usual mean-SHAP explanation admits a justified objection by the coalition {Ratings, ROM, Battery}. In a gradient-boosting forecaster of retail orders the exact game has an empty core and strong higher-order interactions; the nucleolus departs from the Shapley value by up to 0.19 variance shares, and sparse third-order surrogates recover it where pairwise ones cannot.

items.title: Security of Deep Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Driving: A Survey
items.description: arXiv:2212.06123v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables agents to learn optimal behaviors through interaction with their environment and has been increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications, including autonomous driving. Despite its promise, RL is susceptible to attacks designed either to compromise policy learning or to induce erroneous decisions by trained agents. Although the literature on RL security has grown rapidly and several surveys exist, existing categorizations often fall short in guiding the selection of appropriate defenses for specific systems. In this work, we present a comprehensive survey of 86 recent studies on RL security, addressing these limitations by systematically categorizing attacks and defenses according to defined threat models and single- versus multi-agent settings. Furthermore, we examine the relevance and applicability of state-of-the-art attacks and defense mechanisms within the context of autonomous driving, providing insights to inform the design of robust RL systems.

items.title: Active Learning For Contextual Linear Optimization: A Margin-Based Approach
items.description: arXiv:2305.06584v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop the first active learning method for contextual linear optimization. Specifically, we introduce a label acquisition algorithm that sequentially decides whether to request the ``labels'' of feature samples arriving in an unlabeled data stream, where the labels correspond to the objective coefficients in the linear optimization problem. The label acquisition rule is guided by the decision loss induced by the predicted coefficients, known as the Smart Predict-then-Optimize (SPO) loss. Motivated by the structure of the SPO loss, our algorithm uses the distance to degeneracy as a margin-based criterion for label acquisition. The algorithm processes incoming feature samples in batches, acquiring within each batch only the labels of samples whose distance to degeneracy falls below a rejection threshold. We derive non-asymptotic bounds for direct SPO-loss minimization over a general hypothesis class and for surrogate-loss minimization over a linear prediction class. These bounds demonstrate that, under certain natural conditions, our margin-based active learning algorithm requires fewer labels than supervised learning to achieve the same excess population risk for the chosen training loss. We provide concrete examples in which these conditions hold under continuous (sub-)Gaussian noise. Finally, we present numerical evidence demonstrating the practical value of our approach in applications such as personalized pricing and shortest-path problems.

items.title: FlexTSF: A Flexible Forecasting Model for Time Series with Variable Regularities
items.description: arXiv:2410.23160v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generalizing across time series with irregular temporal structures poses a persistent challenge for universal time series forecasting models. Existing approaches often assume regular sampling or depend heavily on imputation, which limits their applicability in real-world scenarios where irregularities are prevalent due to diverse sensing devices and recording practices. To address this gap, we propose FlexTSF, a flexible and domain-adaptive forecasting model specifically designed for time series with variable temporal regularities. At its foundation lies the IVP Patcher, a continuous-time patching module leveraging Initial Value Problems (IVPs) to inherently handle uneven sampling intervals, variable sequence lengths, and missing values. Built upon a decoder-only Transformer architecture, FlexTSF integrates normalized timestamp inputs and domain-specific statistical descriptors through a specialized causal self-attention mechanism, enabling adaptability across domains. Extensive experiments on 16 datasets demonstrate FlexTSF's effectiveness, significantly outperforming existing models in classic forecasting scenarios, zero-shot generalization, and low-resource fine-tuning conditions.

items.title: Almost Sure Convergence Rates and Concentration of Stochastic Approximation and Reinforcement Learning with Markovian Noise
items.description: arXiv:2411.13711v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper establishes, to our knowledge, the first almost sure convergence rate and the first maximal concentration bound with sub-Weibull tails for general contractive stochastic approximation algorithms with Markovian noise. As a corollary, we also obtain convergence rates in $L^p$. Key to our successes is a novel discretization of the mean ODE of stochastic approximation algorithms using intervals with diminishing (instead of constant) length. Applications yield the first almost sure convergence rate for $Q$-learning without count-based learning rates and the first maximal concentration bound for off-policy temporal difference learning, both with Markovian samples.

items.title: Learning with Local Search MCMC Layers
items.description: arXiv:2505.14240v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Integrating combinatorial optimization layers into neural networks has recently attracted significant research interest. However, many existing approaches lack theoretical guarantees or fail to perform adequately when relying on inexact solvers. This is a critical limitation, as many operations research problems are NP-hard, often necessitating the use of neighborhood-based local search heuristics. In this paper, we introduce a principled approach for learning with such inexact solvers. Inspired by the connection between simulated annealing and Metropolis-Hastings, we transform the problem specific neighborhood systems used in local search heuristics into proposal distributions, implementing MCMC on the set of feasible solutions. This allows us to construct differentiable, stochastic combinatorial layers and associated loss functions. Replacing an exact solver with a local search strongly reduces the computational burden of learning on many applications. We demonstrate our approach on a dynamic vehicle routing problem with time windows, binary vector and k-subset prediction tasks, as well as a multi-dimensional knapsack decision-focused learning problem.

items.title: TabPFN: One Model to Rule Them All?
items.description: arXiv:2505.20003v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hollmann et al. (Nature 637 (2025) 319-326) recently introduced TabPFN, a transformer-based deep learning model for regression and classification on tabular data, which they claim "outperforms all previous methods on datasets with up to 10,000 samples by a wide margin, using substantially less training time." Furthermore, they have called TabPFN a "foundation model" for tabular data, as it can support "data generation, density estimation, learning reusable embeddings and fine-tuning". In this paper, we provide a tailored explanation of how TabPFN works for a statistics audience, by emphasizing its interpretation as approximate Bayesian inference. We then explore the significance of TabPFN to the field of statistics: We show that an out-of-the-box application of TabPFN can sometimes outperform specialized state-of-the-art methods for semi-supervised parameter estimation, prediction under covariate shift, and heterogeneous treatment effect estimation. As a partial explanation for the predictive effectiveness of TabPFN, we show that it can simultaneously adapt to both nonparametric structure and parametric structure, for instance, sometimes outperforming LASSO even when assumptions are correctly specified. All experiments can be reproduced using the code provided at https://github.com/qinglong-tian/tabpfn_study (https://github.com/qinglong-tian/tabpfn_study).

items.title: SCAR: State-Space Compression for AI-Based Radio Resource Management of Vehicular Services
items.description: arXiv:2508.06243v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The increasing demand for connected vehicular services poses significant challenges for AI-based network and service management due to the high volume and rapid variability of network state information. Traditional management and control mechanisms struggle to scale when processing fine-grained metrics such as Channel Quality Indicators (CQIs) in dynamic vehicular environments. To address this challenge, we propose SCAR (State-Space Compression for AI-Based Radio Resource Management), an edge-assisted framework that abstracts high-dimensional CQI information into compact representations for AI-based management.
